n: One of the most beautiful images in scripture: water flows out from under the temple’s threshold, eastward past the altar. Life-giving blessing springs from the place of God’s presence. Joseph Smith taught that this prophecy would be fulfilled in the last days with a temple in Jerusalem.

f.w: waters issued out from under the threshold of the house

n: The east gate is shut, so the guide leads Ezekiel out the north gate and around to see the stream trickling out on the south side of the east gate.

f.g: Hebrew suggests a trickle, as if from a small flask—the stream starts tiny.

n: About a third of a mile downstream, the water is ankle-deep. Ezekiel wades through it himself.
Every thousand cubits the water rises—knee-deep, then waist-deep—with no tributaries feeding it. God’s blessing grows in ways nature cannot explain.
Finally it becomes a river too deep to cross—water to swim in. What began as a trickle becomes overwhelming abundance.
“Have you seen this?” The guide wants Ezekiel to grasp the meaning, then leads him back to the riverbank.
Ezekiel now notices many trees lining both banks—an oasis in what was once desert.
The river flows east through the barren Judean wilderness down to the Dead Sea, whose salty water will be made fresh. A dead sea comes to life.

f.g: The Dead Sea, so salty that almost nothing lives in it.

n: Wherever the river goes, life follows—swarms of creatures and abundant fish. It is a picture of how God’s presence brings life to everything it touches.

f.w: every thing shall live whither the river cometh

n: Fishermen will line the shore from En-gedi to En-eglaim, drying their nets, with as many kinds of fish as the Mediterranean. En-gedi is an oasis on the Dead Sea’s western shore.

f.g: A spring and oasis on the west shore of the Dead Sea.

n: Some marshes will stay salty—useful as a source of salt, an important resource. Not everything changes, but what remains has purpose.

Fruit trees on both banks never wither and bear fresh fruit every month. Their fruit nourishes and their leaves heal—because their water comes from the sanctuary. Revelation picks up this image for the tree of life.

f.w: because their waters they issued out of the sanctuary

n: Now God sets the boundaries of the land for the twelve tribes. Joseph gets two portions—one for each of his sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as Jacob had promised.
The land is divided equally among the tribes, fulfilling God’s oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

f.w: I lifted up mine hand to give it unto your fathers

n: The northern border runs from the Mediterranean inland toward Hethlon and Zedad, in the region of modern Lebanon and Syria.
More northern landmarks are listed, around Hamath and Damascus. These match the ideal borders described in Moses’ day.

f.g: A city on the Orontes River in Syria, marking Israel’s ideal northern limit.

n: The northern line ends at Hazar-enan, near the border of Damascus.
The eastern border is the Jordan River down to the Dead Sea. Notably, the land east of the Jordan (Gilead) is not included.
The southern border runs from Tamar to the springs of Kadesh, then along the Brook of Egypt to the Mediterranean.

f.w: the waters of strife in Kadesh
f.g: Meribah-Kadesh, where Israel quarreled with Moses over water.
The Wadi of Egypt, a seasonal stream in the northern Sinai.

n: The western border is the Mediterranean coast.
The land is to be divided among the tribes of Israel according to these borders.
A remarkable provision: foreigners who live among Israel and raise families there receive an inheritance just like native-born Israelites. God’s people include those who join them.

f.w: to the strangers that sojourn among you

n: The stranger receives land within whatever tribe he lives among—fully integrated into the covenant people.
